opus-5.5.text:
I think you need both, but I'd lean toward teaching more than people expect. One thing I've seen at AI Fund is that the founders who do well have strong instincts about the technology and the customer. Those instincts are very hard to outsource. If you're building an AI product and you don't understand what the models can and can't do, you'll make bad product decisions. You'll promise things the technology can't deliver, or you'll miss something that's suddenly become easy. So I think founders should learn the essentials. They don't need to become research scientists, but they need enough technical intuition to make fast, good decisions.

At the same time, no one can know everything. Starting a company means doing a hundred things you've never done before: hiring, fundraising, pricing, legal, go-to-market. Trying to master all of that yourself before acting is a recipe for moving too slowly. So we try to surround founders with people who've done it before. Then when they hit a problem, someone can say, "Here's how we handled that last time," and save them a few months of pain.

The way I think about it is that founders should deeply own the few things that drive the company's core decisions. For many AI startups, that's the technology and the customer. Everything else they can get help with. Speed matters so much in startups. Teaching gives you good judgment, and a strong support network lets you act on it quickly. When you get both right, founders move much faster and make far fewer avoidable mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response lists hiring among tasks founders may get help with; it does not say founders must be able to recruit themselves.

r002.rationale: It explicitly leans toward teaching founders more, while presenting a support network as complementary rather than higher leverage.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I actually don't think of those as being in tension. At AI Fund, we do both, and I think you need both.

Here's how I think about it. When we start a company, there's a pretty well-defined set of things that have to happen in the first few months. You have to validate the idea, you have to build something, you have to talk to customers, you have to hire, you have to raise money eventually. And a lot of founders, especially technical founders, are world-class at maybe two of those things and have never done the others. So some of this really is teachable. We've done this enough times now that we have playbooks, we have patterns we've seen work and not work, and I think it would be irresponsible not to pass that on. I've spent a lot of my career teaching, so maybe I'm biased, but I genuinely believe that a founder who understands, say, how to run a disciplined customer discovery process will just move faster than one who's figuring it out from scratch.

But there's a limit to how much you can learn from a lecture or a document. A lot of what makes a company work is tacit. It's judgment. It's knowing when the data says one thing but your gut says something else and which one to trust. And that you mostly get from people who've been through it. So we surround our founders with experienced operators, with domain experts, with people who've built go-to-market in that specific industry. If you're building a company in, I don't know, maritime logistics, no amount of general startup training replaces talking to someone who's actually sold into shipping companies for twenty years.

The way I'd put it is, teaching compresses the time to competence on the things that are generalizable. Surrounding people with the right network handles the things that aren't. And honestly, the best founders I've worked with are the ones who are hungry for both. They want to learn the skill, and they also know exactly which questions they can't answer themselves and go find the person who can.

One more thing I'd add. There's a failure mode where you surround founders with so many advisors that they stop making their own decisions. That's dangerous. So part of what we try to teach is actually how to use advisors well, how to extract the insight and then still own the call. Because at the end of the day, it's their company.

r001.rationale: The response lists hiring as something a startup must do and says founders can be taught skills, but it does not clearly identify recruiting as a skill founders themselves must be able to perform.

r002.rationale: The response says teaching and surrounding founders with experienced people are both needed, assigning them different roles. It does not judge surrounding founders as the higher-leverage approach.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as complementary. A founder doesn’t need to be the best person at every function, but they need enough understanding to make good decisions about whom to hire, what to delegate, and whether things are working.

Take sales. If you’re a technical founder, you may eventually hire someone who’s much better at sales than you are. But spending time talking to customers yourself teaches you things that are hard to get secondhand: what problem people actually have, what they’ll pay for, and why they hesitate. That learning helps you hire and work with a sales leader.

So I’d ask: Is this a skill the founder needs in order to learn about the business and exercise judgment? If so, it’s worth teaching. If it’s specialized execution that someone else can do much better, bring that person in. And often the fastest way to build the founder’s judgment is to have them work alongside someone experienced on a real problem.

r001.rationale: The response says founders need enough understanding to decide whom to hire, but does not identify recruiting as a skill they must perform themselves.

r002.rationale: The response calls teaching and bringing in experienced people complementary and recommends each in different situations; it does not judge surrounding founders with helpers to be higher leverage than teaching them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need both. A founder needs enough understanding to make good decisions, but they don’t need to become the best person at every function in the company. The question is: what do you need to learn yourself, and where should you bring in someone with deeper expertise?

For an AI startup, for example, a founder should understand enough about the technology to have a useful conversation about what’s feasible and how to evaluate whether a product is working. You can hire a great engineer, but you still need to exercise judgment about what to build.

And surrounding yourself with good people actually helps you learn. So I wouldn’t frame teaching and building a team as competing approaches. Teach founders the skills that help them ask better questions, then surround them with people who can help them answer those questions and execute.

r001.rationale: The response says founders should bring in people with deeper expertise, but does not identify recruiting as a skill founders must perform themselves.

r002.rationale: It presents teaching and building a team as complementary approaches and does not judge surrounding founders with people as higher leverage than teaching them skills.
